prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Every, Because, Hispanics

outputs.L1: My ocean town struggles to gather its fallen leaves, to offer summer school, and to keep our library open. Each day now, more men gather at the railroad station, waiting to be chosen for work. Because it is believed that the Hispanics will labor for less, they are picked first, while the whites and blacks avert their eyes from the terror they see in one another's. Our handyman, Santos, who expects only what his hands can earn, takes pride in his half acre in Guatemala, where he intends to retire. His desire to proceed with dignity is admirable, yet he knows that now no one retires; everyone simply works harder. My father imagined a life more fulfilling than the one he managed to lead. He did not see himself as uneducated, thwarted, or embittered, but as soon-to-be rich. Being rich, he believed, was his birthright. Happiness, I once thought, was a necessary illusion. Now I believe it is merely fleeting moments of relief, like dreams of Guatemala. Sometimes, on winter nights, surrounded by the profound silence of empty mansions—which were once cottages, where people lived out their lives, and are now owned by banks and the absent rich—I like to stand at my window, searching for the futile flicker of a television, only to be surprised, always, by the quaint, porous face of my own reflection instead, immersed in its solitary abundance.
outputs.L2:
My seaside community can barely manage to collect fallen leaves, provide summer classes, or maintain operating hours at our library. These days, the crowd of men gathering at the train depot grows larger, all hoping to be selected for a day's labor. Since employers assume Hispanic workers will accept lower wages, they're the first to be hired, leaving the white and black men to look away from the fear reflected in each other's faces. Santos, the man who does our repairs, asks for nothing beyond what he can earn through his own labor, and he takes pride in the small plot of land he owns in Guatemala, where retirement awaits him. There's something admirable in his wish to carry himself with dignity, yet he understands the reality: retirement has become impossible, and everyone simply toils more than before.

My father pictured for himself a more rewarding existence than the one he actually lived. He never regarded himself as poorly schooled, frustrated, or resentful—only as a man on the verge of wealth. In his mind, prosperity was something he was entitled to. There was a time when I believed happiness to be a necessary deception. These days, I've come to see it differently—as nothing more than fleeting instants of comfort, not unlike Santos's dreams of Guatemala.

On occasion, during winter nights, I find myself enveloped by the heavy quiet of vacant mansions—buildings that were once modest cottages sheltering ordinary lives, but now belong to banks and to wealthy owners who never appear. In those moments, I position myself at my window, hoping to catch the pointless glow of a television somewhere, only to be caught off guard each time by what greets me instead: the odd, weathered features of my own reflection, absorbed in the single richness it possesses.
outputs.L3:
# A Town by the Ocean

The ocean town where I grew up has fallen on hard times. The money simply isn't there anymore—not for the small things that once made a place feel cared for. The leaves gather in the gutters through autumn because no one comes to collect them. Summer school has been canceled, its classrooms dark through the season when children most need somewhere to go. Even the library, that quiet refuge, can no longer afford to keep its doors open. These are not luxuries but the basic services that hold a community together, and one by one they have slipped away.

In the labor market that remains, a quiet cruelty has taken root. Hispanic workers are called first for the jobs, chosen ahead of others because employers believe they will accept lower wages without complaint. This assumption breeds a poisonous tension among everyone who needs work. White, black, and Hispanic laborers alike live under a shared fear—each watching the others, each wondering who will be passed over next. The scarcity turns neighbors into competitors and makes suspicion a condition of survival.

Santos, the handyman, carries a modest dream through all of this. He owns a half acre of land back in Guatemala, and he imagines returning there someday to retire with dignity, to rest on soil that is his own. Yet even he understands the illusion in that hope. In this economy, he knows, no one truly retires. There is no soft landing, no final rest—only the endless demand to work harder, to keep going, to squeeze out a living for as long as the body allows. His dream and his clear-eyed knowledge exist side by side, neither one able to erase the other.

My father, too, lived by a saving illusion. He believed, without evidence and against all odds, that he was destined to become rich. He refused to see himself as others might have—as an uneducated man, as someone the world had left behind, as a person with reason to be bitter. That refusal was its own kind of strength. Watching him, I came to understand something about the nature of happiness: how often it rests not on truth but on the stories we tell ourselves, on the comforting fictions that let us rise each morning and believe the future still owes us something.

And so I return, in my mind, to the cottages along the shore. Once they were full of life—small, warm places where families gathered and summers unfolded. Now many of them have been torn down or transformed into vast, vacant mansions, owned by banks or by the absent rich who never come to live in them. They stand empty, monuments to a wealth that has no warmth in it. Walking among them, I feel the loss of what was here before. And yet, strangely, I find a quiet abundance in my own solitude—in the simple fact of my reflection, my presence, my capacity to notice and to remember. It is not much, but in a landscape hollowed out by absence, it is something that is genuinely mine.
outputs.L4:
# The Ocean Town

The gulls still circle here, above the harbor
where fishing boats once crowded the gray water,
their painted hulls now flaking in the salt air.
This is my town, and I have come to know it
the way you know a face grown old with hardship—
each line a story, each scar a small defeat.

Down by the docks, the immigrants arrive
before the sun, their voices low and foreign,
carrying the weight of other countries
in the calloused patience of their hands.
They gut the fish, they haul the nets, they scrub
the decks of boats they'll never come to own.
I watch them and I wonder what they dreamed
before this shore, before the promised plenty
dissolved into these wages barely earned,
these rooms they share three families to a floor.
The town divides itself along old fractures—
who speaks the language, who arrived, who stays,
whose children will be welcomed in the schools.

My father worked these waters all his life.
He came here believing what they told him:
that effort earns reward, that decent men
who rise at dawn and give their honest labor
will one day rest in comfort they have built.
I remember how he stood each evening
looking out across the darkening bay,
his silence growing heavier each year
as the boats sold off, as the canneries closed,
as everything he'd trusted came to nothing.
He never spoke of it directly—no,
he was not a man who spoke his sorrows—
but I could read the disappointment there,
the slow surrender in his lowered shoulders,
a lifetime measured out and found still wanting.

Above the town, along the cliffside road,
the mansions stand like monuments to absence.
Once they belonged to families, to laughter
spilling from lit windows in the summer.
Now they are owned by banks, by distant men
whose names appear on documents alone,
who never walk these rooms or watch these sunsets.
The lawns grow wild. The shutters hang and knock
against the wind. The pools have long gone green.
These are the empty temples of the wealthy,
the American Dream turned mausoleum,
proof that the promise, even when fulfilled,
can hollow out to nothing but a shell.

And so I have been thinking about happiness—
not as the glossy image we were sold,
not as the mansion or the fattened bank account,
not as the endless upward climb they promised.
That kind of happiness was always fiction,
a story told to keep us moving forward,
to keep us laboring toward a horizon
that pulled away each time we thought we'd reached it.

No—happiness, I think, is something smaller.
It is the moment when the morning light
falls warm across the kitchen table.
It is the sudden, unexpected relief
when a burden lifts, however briefly.
It is the instant when I catch my breath
and recognize myself, still here, still standing,
in a town that disappointment has not broken.
It is my father's rare and sudden laughter,
the immigrants who sing while mending nets,
the stubborn beauty that survives despite it all.

This is the quiet resilience that I've found:
not triumph, not the winning of the world,
but the small persistence of the human heart
in places that the promised dream forgot—
the fleeting, precious moments of relief,
the recognition of ourselves as whole,
even amid the wreckage and the loss,
even here, in this forgotten town beside the sea.

# The Growing Influence of Hispanics in America

**Every** day, the Hispanic community continues to shape the cultural, economic, and social landscape of the United States. From the vibrant streets of Miami to the bustling neighborhoods of Los Angeles, the contributions of Hispanics can be seen in nearly every aspect of American life.

**Because** of their rich heritage and strong family values, Hispanics have become an essential part of the nation's identity. Their traditions—expressed through food, music, language, and celebrations—have enriched communities across the country. Whether it's the flavors of authentic cuisine or the rhythms of Latin music, these cultural elements have found a permanent home in American society.

The economic impact is equally significant. **Every** year, Hispanic-owned businesses generate billions of dollars and create countless jobs. These entrepreneurs demonstrate remarkable resilience and ambition, often building successful enterprises from the ground up. **Because** of their determination and hard work, many have achieved the American dream and inspired future generations to pursue their own goals.

Education and civic participation are also areas where growth is evident. **Every** election cycle, more Hispanic voters make their voices heard, influencing policies that affect their communities and the nation as a whole. **Because** their numbers continue to rise, political leaders increasingly recognize the importance of addressing issues that matter to this diverse population.

Looking toward the future, it's clear that Hispanics will play an ever-larger role in defining what it means to be American. **Every** contribution, whether large or small, adds to a shared story of diversity and progress that benefits everyone.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem about economic inequality in a coastal town, told from the perspective of a homeowner observing day laborers and reflecting on their own father's failed dreams of wealth.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Tide Brings**

From my window I watch them gather
at the corner where Delgado's market used to be,
before the renovation, before the espresso,
before the word *artisanal* washed up here
like something the ocean couldn't stomach.

The men wait in the blue hour,
lunch pails, thermoses, the particular patience
of those who have learned that hope
is a muscle you exercise or lose.

A truck stops. Three are chosen.
The rest fold back into themselves,
and I sip my coffee, ashamed
of the warmth of my kitchen,
the deed with my name pressed into it
like a thumbprint in wet clay.

My father wanted this—
not this house, but the idea of it,
the arrival. He kept a ledger
of schemes: the marina that never dredged,
the seafood distributorship,
the parcel of land he bought on a handshake
that turned out to be underwater
half the tidal day.

He died renting.
He died certain the next season
would be the one, the way these men
must believe in the next truck,
the next corner, the next country even.

I did nothing to earn this view.
I inherited timing, a market that swelled
beneath me like a friendly wave
while it crashed on everyone waiting
at Delgado's corner in the cold.

The difference between us
is not effort. My father proved that,
sweating over his ledgers,
his beautiful doomed arithmetic.
The difference is the tide,
which lifts some boats
and leaves others in the mud,
gasping, gleaming, going nowhere.

By noon the corner empties.
The unchosen drift toward home,
wherever the sea has permitted them one.
And I stand here, a man
in a house he did not build,
watching the water
take back what it lends,
and lend again,
and never once ask
who deserves to stay dry.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a reflective poem that touches on immigration, class divides between whites, blacks, and Hispanics, and the loneliness of empty mansions once owned by ordinary people.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Empty Houses Know**

The realtor's sign leans in the yard,
its paint gone soft in August rain—
another family packed and gone,
another door that won't unchain.

They built these rooms with modest hands,
a schoolteacher, a man who welded steel,
who thought the mortgage was a promise
that the ground beneath was real.

Now the mansions on the hillside stand
like teeth in an unsmiling mouth,
the wealthy fled to somewhere colder,
the workers drifted further south.

Maria crosses at first light
to clean the glass of houses where
no one sleeps, no children run—
she wipes the emptiness with care,

and thinks of borders she once crossed,
the desert's patient, killing sun,
to reach a country that had rooms
enough for everyone, or none.

Down the road, old Thompson sits,
a Black man on a whitewashed porch,
who watched the factories go dark
and felt his pension's dimming torch.

He nods at James, the neighbor's son,
whose father lost the union card—
two men divided by a line
some other hand had drawn too hard.

And who was told to fear the other?
And who profited from all the fear?
The empty houses do not answer,
though they have watched us disappear.

The wind moves through the vacant halls
where ordinary lives once burned—
a wedding dance, a baby's cry,
the lessons that we never learned.

Perhaps the loneliness we build
is just the sum of all our walls,
the immigrant, the exile, all of us
haunting the same empty halls.

So let me leave a light on here,
in one bright window, small and warm—
a signal to whoever comes,
still human, weathering the storm.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the voice of a middle-class narrator in a struggling ocean town, mentioning a Guatemalan handyman named Santos and meditating on happiness, dignity, and disillusionment.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Handyman's Hands

The gutters sag along my rented street
where fishing boats once crowded at the pier.
Now half the storefronts wear their FOR LEASE signs
like widows' veils. I've lived here fifteen years.

Santos came Tuesday, fixed my kitchen faucet,
the one that dripped a metronome of doubt
through sleepless nights. He worked without complaint,
his hands more certain than my own about

the way a thing gets mended. "Bueno," he said,
and wiped the wrench, and would not take the extra
I pressed on him. I watched him load his truck—
Guatemala in the rearview, some old letter

folded in the visor. What does he carry?
I used to think that happiness arrived
like weather, something owed to those who waited.
My father's pension promised. I survived

the layoffs, kept the house, kept up appearances,
and still the tide goes out and doesn't turn.
Santos hums a song I do not know.
There is a dignity I've yet to learn

in doing well the small, unglamorous work—
the honest weld, the level shelf, the seal
that holds. I wanted meaning handed down.
He builds his, quietly, from what is real.

The ocean doesn't care that we're diminished,
that the cannery is condos now, the young
all gone to cities. Still the mornings come.
Still someone tunes a faucet like a tongue

to speak in water's plain, forgiving language.
I stand here in my doorway, middle-aged,
and watch his taillights vanish toward the highway—
a man who owns his labor, and his wage,

and something more I've bartered off for comfort
and called it being reasonable. The sea
keeps folding, folding, like a hand of cards
I thought I understood. Santos is free

in ways I'm only starting to consider.
The faucet doesn't drip. The night is whole.
I lie awake and count what I've been given
against the smaller, harder word: my soul.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a contemplative poem about the decline of a small seaside community—cut services, unemployed men at the railroad station, and the narrator's late-night solitude at the window.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Station at Low Tide**

They took the ferry first, then the clinic,
then the little library where I learned my letters—
one by one, like teeth pulled from a slack jaw,
the town gives up what made it able to speak.

Down at the railroad station the men still gather,
though nothing comes or goes on the rusted line.
They stand in the salt wind with their hands
grown strange to them, these hands that hauled
and mended, coiled the wet rope, gutted the catch.
Now they hold only the cold of morning,
passing it between them like a shared cigarette,
saying little, watching the empty tracks
as if a train might yet arrive
and ask them, please, to lift and carry.

I know their faces from the church, the pier,
the years when herring silvered every net.
Their fathers built these houses to outlast them.
Their sons have taken the road out and stayed gone.

At night I keep my window like a lamp
no ship requires. The harbor holds its dark.
The last streetlight the council left us
throws a coin of yellow on the wet stones
and asks for nothing back.

I am the only wakefulness for miles,
or so it feels—the town a held breath
beneath the turning, indifferent stars.
Somewhere the sea goes on unmaking the shore
grain by patient grain, the way a place
forgets itself: not all at once,
but service by service, light by light,
until the map keeps a name
the living can no longer fill.

Still I sit. Still the kettle ticks its cooling.
Still, past the glass, the tide comes in
to touch the pilings where the boats once rode,
and goes out again, and takes a little with it,
and leaves the rest for morning to decide.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a literary poem exploring themes of money, retirement, immigrant labor, and self-reflection, ending with the narrator seeing their own face in a window instead of a television's glow.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Window Keeps

My father counted coins the way some men count prayers,
each nickel a small country he had crossed to reach,
each dollar folded twice and pressed between the pages
of a bible he could barely read but wouldn't sell.

He came here with a language in his mouth like gravel,
laid brick until the mortar wrote itself
into the creases of his palms. *Retirement*, he'd say,
rolling the word around like something foreign,

a fruit he'd heard of but had never tasted.
Thirty years of scaffolding and cold lunch pails,
of sending half of everything back home
to mothers, sisters, ghosts across an ocean.

Now I sit in the apartment that his labor built—
though not for him, never for him, but for the ledger
of some landlord's grandson—and I watch the hours
pool like water in the low place of the evening.

I have his hands. I notice this too late.
The money I have made is cleaner, quieter,
arriving in numbers on a lit screen,
untouched by weather, unremembered by the body.

What have I bought that he would recognize?
Not rest. Not the country that he thought he entered.
Only this: the same arithmetic of want,
the same subtraction dressed in better clothes.

Tonight I meant to lose myself in the blue glow,
to let some story rinse me of my own,
but the television stayed a black rectangle,
and in its place, against the window's dark,

I found a face. My father's, or my own—
the difference thinning with each passing year—
lit faintly by the streetlamp's tired gold,
watching me watch it, asking what I saved,

and what I spent, and whether any of it
was ever mine to keep, or only borrowed
like breath, like light, like the long shift of a life
that ends the way it started: looking out, and in.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
